diagnostics.notes: Both claims accurately reflect their sources: side A reports a negative irisin-glucose correlation (r = -0.259; p = 0.039) in a Brazilian adult cohort grouped by BMI; side B reports a significant positive irisin-glucose correlation (p < 0.001) in adolescents/young adults with PCOS and controls. Exposure (circulating irisin) and outcome (glucose) are sufficiently similar; the contrast is the same association with opposite directions. The populations differ concretely and are text-supported on both sides: A studied predominantly middle-aged adults (mean age 46 ± 14) undergoing cholecystectomy or gastric bypass in Southern Brazil, while B studied adolescents and young adults with polycystic ovarian syndrome, a condition defined by insulin resistance, versus controls. B's background also notes prior reports of elevated irisin in adult PCOS. This population difference is a plausible, source-supported contextual explanation for the opposite correlation directions; the plasma-versus-serum sample matrix is an additional supported difference.

source_evidence.quote: The study subjects were predominantly female (75%), white (82%), with a mean age of 46 ± 14 years.

Irisin was negatively correlated with weight (r = -0.246; p = 0.042), waist circumference (r = -0.272; p = 0.024), glucose (r = -0.259; p = 0.039), glycated hemoglobin (r = -0.283; p = 0.024), triglycerides (r = -0.414; p = 0.024), and positively correlated with HDL (r = 0.280; p = 0.029).
Polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS) is a prevalent hormonal condition defined by insulin resistance.
The findings revealed a significant positive correlation of serum irisin levels with BMI, glucose, insulin, HOMA-IR, LH, estradiol, and testosterone(all p-values < 0.001).

verdict.label: apparent_contradiction
verdict.rationale: Both extractions are faithful to their sources. Side A reports plasma irisin negatively correlated with glucose (r = -0.259; p = 0.039) in a prospective cohort of predominantly middle-aged adults (mean age 46 ± 14) in Southern Brazil stratified by BMI, while side B reports serum irisin significantly positively correlated with glucose (p < 0.001) in a cross-sectional study of adolescents and young adults with PCOS and controls. The same exposure-outcome association is thus reported in opposite directions. The abstracts supply a concrete, text-supported contextual difference that could explain this: side B's population consists of adolescents/young adults with polycystic ovarian syndrome, a condition the abstract defines by insulin resistance, whereas side A studied a general adult obesity/cholecystectomy-bypass cohort; the sample matrix also differs (plasma vs serum). This supports apparent_contradiction rather than contradictory.
